headline: Millions of Children Are Losing Food Stamps

paragraphs.text: When Republicans pushed record cuts in food stamps through Congress last year, they insisted that one group of Americans would remain unaffected: children.

But as many as two million children have lost benefits, about one in eight who had them, state data suggests. The drop indicates that the reductions in food stamps, championed by President Trump, have affected a broader and more vulnerable population than predicted.

While it is not wholly clear why families with children have lost aid, the decline has been driven in part by incentives in the law for states to demand more proof of eligibility, which some applicants say makes it hard to get help. Tens of millions of people rely on the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or food stamps, making it central to the safety net.

While the cuts were part of a package that included large tax breaks for the wealthy, the overhaul also reflected conservative views that SNAP attracted fraud and discouraged work, hurting people the aid aimed to help. With a decline in SNAP rolls already twice as large as the Congressional Budget Office predicted, the law’s accelerating effects test the idea that a smaller safety net will provide poor people with adequate protection.

The decline in SNAP is especially steep in Louisiana, where enrollment among children has dropped by nearly a quarter since July 2025, when the law passed. With grocery bills at persistent highs, parents losing benefits say that they skip meals to feed children, divert rent money to groceries, serve inexpensive, unhealthy food, and worry to a disturbing degree. Some parents with low wages qualify for SNAP despite working full time.

The strain is evident at the Wilcox Academy of Early Learning, which runs three well-regarded child care centers in New Orleans, a city where Black children are more than 10 times as likely as white children to be poor. Before the cuts, most Wilcox students received SNAP, as did many teachers with children of their own. So many have now lost benefits that parents no longer cater the school festival, and the cook stretches school meals so teachers can take leftovers home.
“They come in asking: Do I have any food for them and their kids?” said the cook, Raymond Brown. “Times are hard if they’re asking me.”

Among those struggling is Ivana Norgah, the gregarious anchor of the toddler room, whose responsibilities include the little people in her lap and a big one at home. At 285 pounds, her son, Kane Mitchell, is a high school lineman with college football hopes.

After losing SNAP in a dispute with the state about whether her fluctuating earnings left her eligible, Ms. Norgah, 43, has become a chronic meal-skipper who pretends she is not hungry when bringing school leftovers to her son. Still, she runs out of staples as basic as peanut butter, and fills him with fast food, at times with loyalty points. “It’s definitely changed the way we eat,” she said.

Mindful of his mother’s feelings, Kane, 16, tries to limit complaints about his grumbling stomach and speaks tactfully of “the red bean situation” — all beans and no meat. “The food — I’m not going to say it’s limited, but it’s, like, limited,” he said.
A Cascade of Consequences

Republicans’ longstanding complaints about SNAP accelerated after the Biden administration unilaterally raised monthly benefits, pushing annual costs above $100 billion. Nearly 42 million Americans received SNAP before the cuts, including 16 million children.

Congress reduced benefits, required more recipients to work, and shifted costs to the states, with new incentives to scrutinize applications. Congressional scorekeepers said the overhaul would cut $187 billion over nine years, or about 20 percent when fully in effect.
In dismissing warnings that children would suffer, Republicans noted that the law’s most prominent feature — the work rules — exempted most families with children.

“If you have young children at home, your benefits are unaffected by this bill,” said Representative Dusty Johnson of South Dakota. Representative Glenn Thompson of Pennsylvania, the chairman of the House Agriculture Committee, said the law would protect “the most vulnerable among us, including children.”

But it ignited large declines among adults and children alike. While only 14 states, including Louisiana, publish children’s caseloads, the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities, a left-leaning research group, compiled unpublished data from others.

Its sample of 29 states, the most comprehensive count, found that the number of children on SNAP had fallen 14 percent since the law passed. Projecting nationwide, the center estimates that enrollment has dropped by 5.7 million people, and two million are children.
Mr. Johnson and Mr. Thompson, the G.O.P. lawmakers, did not respond to requests for comment.

Enrollment is dropping in part because states demand more proof of eligibility. The law imposes large penalties on states that make excessive errors in awarding benefits. Unless Louisiana reduces errors, it will owe $160 million.

Some parents losing aid are eligible and manage to re-enroll. Others give up. Still others are properly disenrolled, with net incomes above the eligibility line (about $27,000 for a family of three), yet struggle to feed their families.
Camille Conaway, who runs SNAP at Louisiana’s health department, said there was no way to know how many people losing aid remained eligible, but the number could be substantial.

“There are tens of thousands of families that probably still qualify for SNAP — they just didn’t stay on the rolls for whatever reason,” she said. “The goal is always: If you’re eligible, reapply, give us the verification and let’s get you back in.”
Eating Less to Feed the Kids

Steneisha Morehead, a Wilcox teacher with three children, lost SNAP last year amid document requests she found “overwhelming.” She thinks a raise of $1 an hour might have left her ineligible. But she remains unsure. Earning $18 to $20 an hour, Wilcox teachers often hover around the SNAP eligibility line.

Without the monthly benefit of $500, Ms. Morehead, 30, skips meals and has stopped offering her children seconds. She is moving in with her sister, who has SNAP, in hopes of eating more and worrying less. “It’s always on my mind — ‘Am I going to have enough?’” she said.

Another Wilcox teacher, Jennifer James, lost SNAP, got it back and lost it again — a confusing sequence, she said, since her income did not change. Ms. James, 36, said her children had not complained about the switch from produce to processed food. But it has aggravated her lupus disease. Her face burns, her lips swell, and “my chest tightens up like I can’t breathe,” she said.
Chesshiara George, a former Wilcox teacher, lost SNAP for five months. She failed to file proof of her earnings, she said, but the state lost other documents.
Without her $400 monthly benefit, Ms. George, 35, skipped meals, scoured food pantries and sold blood plasma to buy groceries. She calls her guilt and depression about her son’s diet “life altering.”

When the boy, a 5-year-old enthralled with superheroes, noticed her fasting and offered to share, she provided reassurance. Eat up “because you’re a superhero,” she said. “You can save the world for me.”
Bionca Fleury, a Wilcox parent, went nine months without SNAP while trying to confirm eligibility for herself and three daughters. “I was worried every day — ‘What am I going to cook?’” she said.
Her eventual success in reclaiming help, like that of Ms. George, reinforces the idea that eligible families are losing aid.

Her cousin lost SNAP after the state said it was missing wage statements that she insisted she had sent. One argument for safety net programs is that they may protect single mothers from depending on abusive men. A single mother with three children, including a disabled daughter, Ms. Fleury’s cousin began accepting groceries from a man seeking romance. Now, she said, “it’s almost like I’ve got a stalker.”
She regrets his expectations, but not the food.
“I’m a mom. I’m going to do what I have to do,” she said.
Fraud or Red Tape?
Louisiana’s SNAP rolls have lost about 6,000 children a month under the new law.

Ms. Conaway, the state official, noted several potential explanations. Better jobs might have raised parents’ incomes. New work rules (for parents of children 14 or older) might have encouraged employment.

Requests for more proof of eligibility also played a role, she said, with the state demanding written proof of rent and paying a data broker, Equifax, to verify wages. “That’s part of it, yes,” she said. “It’s not aimed at closing anyone’s case — it’s aimed at getting the payment right” and avoiding penalties.

Notably, the state conducts an extra review of working households, because their fluctuating incomes increase the risk of payment errors. Since many working-aged households have children, the review means that the children’s aid that lawmakers vowed to protect tends to face added scrutiny.
Angela Rachidi of the conservative American Enterprise Institute said that much of the decline was likely due to “fewer ineligible households receiving aid,” rather than problems with red tape.

Under previous rules, she said, states had little incentive for strict oversight, since the federal government paid benefits and rarely punished mistakes. Facing the threat of penalties, she said “states were forced to tighten up eligibility.”

While the transition off aid can be difficult, “if you have limits, you have to follow them,” she said. “The solution isn’t to rely on one program to eliminate all hardship. The solution is to create a system of upward mobility.”

Some SNAP critics see falling enrollment as evidence that the program suffered from fraud. Fraud does exist, in a program so large. A friend of Ms. Fleury’s who lost SNAP acknowledged that she was “fabricating” — understating her income to get benefits.

But Ms. Conaway said that most payment errors had come from unintended mistakes, by caseworkers and clients alike, amid complex questions about income and expenses. “In general, payment errors are not fraud,” she said. “The volume is tremendous, and it’s just really hard to get it right.”
‘This too shall pass’

On a recent afternoon, Ms. Norgah, the toddler teacher, arrived at her son’s football practice with precious cargo — chicken and rice from the Wilcox kitchen. “He’s going to love what’s in that pan!” she said.

Like many parents short on food, Ms. Norgah tells herself she can spare her child by eating less. But the reality is more complex. Kane says “I’m hungry” so often that she jokes: “Your name’s not ‘hungry’ — it’s Kane.”

Kane ambled to the car, the hulking star of a contact sport happy to see his mom. Asked to describe their refrigerator, he repeated the word “no” — no juice, no waffles, no neck bones in the beans. Had he gone hungry because they lacked food? He hesitated to upset Ms. Norgah, but said, “Yeah, kind of — I’m not going to lie.”
Then he praised her efforts to keep him fed. “She cares about me eating even more than I care about me eating,” he said.

They both coped by making believe. Ms. Norgah knew she could not fully protect Kane, but told herself she could. Kane knew that his mother skipped meals to feed him, but told himself she did not. “I manipulate my mind to think past it, to pretend she’s full,” he said. “I don’t want to go and be another burden.”
“Never feel like that!” Ms. Norgah said.
“I love my mom,” he said. “I don’t want people to think I come from a bad household.”
Ms. Norgah cried. She allowed herself a boast. When Kane’s teammate texted a picture of his empty refrigerator, Kane found five dollars to send.

The sun had set on an empty field, and the chicken awaited. A gladiator on the gridiron and a man of faith off it, Kane offered a departing thought. “This, too, shall pass,” he said. Then mother and son drove home to eat.
